intuition: Choose one current value from every sorted list. Their smallest and largest values define a range covering all lists. To make that range better, advance the list containing the smallest current value. A heap finds that minimum, while a saved maximum gives the other boundary.

To improve this range, advance the list that supplies its minimum. Advancing another representative cannot raise the lower endpoint and cannot reduce the upper endpoint, so it cannot produce a better range before the current minimum changes. A min heap locates the next list to advance, while a separate high value tracks the largest representative.

Each popped minimum yields a valid candidate before its list advances. Compare candidates by width first and left endpoint second, since equal-width ties must favor the earlier range. Sorted lists mean replacement values never move backward, so high only needs to increase.
If the minimum’s list has no successor, stop: proceeding would drop that list’s coverage, and no later covering selection is possible. The heap remains one entry per list throughout the search.

steps: For the three example lists, representatives [4,0,5] produce initial range [0,5].
Advance the list supplying 0 to 9; then advance the list supplying 4 to 10.
Continue advancing only the smallest representative, exposing 18,12,15,20,24,22 in sequence.
Eventually the representatives are 24 from list 0, 20 from list 1, and 22 from list 2.
Their range [20,24] has width 4, improving the earlier width-5 best.
Popping 20 exhausts list 1, so stop and return [20,24].

keyDecision: Stop when a list runs out, because later choices would no longer cover every list.

concept.question: Why must we advance the list currently supplying the minimum?
intuition: Trying every combination of representatives from all lists is enormous. With sorted lists, a current representative from each list gives a complete covering range, and only moving its minimum can raise the lower endpoint.

Keep one current value from every list, compare their minimum, and track their maximum. Record that range, then advance the list that supplied the minimum. Stop when that list has no next value, since further complete frontiers are impossible.
concept.observation: Every candidate frontier includes one representative from each list.
approach: Start at each list’s first value.
Advance the minimum’s list and continue until one list is exhausted.
concept.correctness: For a fixed minimum representative, advancing any other list cannot improve the lower endpoint and cannot lower the maximum. Thus all potentially better ranges arise by advancing the minimum’s list. The process visits those necessary frontiers in order and records their best range. When a list exhausts at the minimum, no larger lower endpoint can still cover that list.

complexity.explanation: Each advance processes one list entry with a logarithmic operation over the number of lists. Work is total processed entries times that logarithm; the frontier stores one entry per list.

pitfalls: Every candidate frontier includes one representative from each list.
